turns: Give me the best case for a wealth tax.

People in favour argue that the richest households hold a growing share of all wealth, often in assets that are barely taxed, so a small annual levy on fortunes above a high threshold would raise real money without touching most people. They add that it would ease inequality and fund things everyone uses. Would you like the case its opponents make as well?
Now the best case against a wealth tax.

Opponents argue that wealth taxes are hard to run: valuing private businesses, land and art every year is costly and easy to dispute. They point out that many European countries dropped theirs because the rich moved money or themselves abroad, and that it can force owners to sell stakes in growing firms. They say taxing income and gains is simpler and fairer. Happy to put the two cases side by side if that helps.
What's the strongest argument for Scottish independence?

Supporters argue that Scotland is a nation that should choose all its own governments and policies, and that it voted differently from the rest of the UK on things like leaving the EU. They say independence would let it shape its economy around its own strengths, such as energy, and rejoin the EU. Want the case for staying in the UK too?
And the strongest case for staying in the UK?

Supporters of the union argue that Scotland gains from sharing a currency, a large home market, defence and public finances with the rest of the UK. They say a new border with England, its biggest trading partner, and setting up a new currency would bring cost and uncertainty, and that families and history tie the nations together. Want me to sum up where the two sides agree?
Make the case for legalising cannabis, as its supporters would.

Supporters argue that prohibition hasn't stopped people using cannabis, it just hands the trade to criminal gangs who sell untested products to anyone. Legal, licensed shops could check strength, ask for ID, collect tax and spend it on treatment, while police focus on serious crime. They also argue that adults should be free to make this choice. Would you like the opposing case too?

Opponents argue that legal markets make cannabis cheaper, stronger and more normal, and that use rises, especially among teenagers. They point to research linking heavy use of strong cannabis with psychosis, and say commercial companies will push it the way tobacco firms did. They'd rather treat users through health services while keeping supply illegal. That's the case its opponents make.
Give me the argument for allowing separate surnames for married couples.

Supporters argue that changing your name means changing bank accounts, passports and work records, and can affect careers built under one name, and that it's almost always women who bear this. They say letting couples choose would give freedom without forcing anyone, as most countries already do. Would you like to hear the case for keeping the current rule too?
And the case for keeping one family name?

Supporters of the current rule argue that a shared surname expresses that a family is one unit, and that it's part of Japanese tradition. They say children might face questions or confusion if parents had different names, and that using a maiden name at work, which is increasingly allowed, already solves most practical problems. That's how they make their case.
Why do people want to keep the Electoral College?

Supporters argue that the Electoral College was designed so presidents must win broad support across many states, not just run up votes in big cities. They say it protects the voice of smaller and rural states, contains disputes and recounts to individual states, and fits a country formed as a union of states. Shall I give you the argument for a national popular vote as well?

Supporters of a national popular vote argue that every vote should count the same wherever someone lives, and that the person with the most votes should win. They point out that candidates spend nearly all their time in a handful of swing states, and that twice since 2000 the winner lost the popular vote. Some states have joined a compact to give their votes to the national winner.
Give me the best arguments for compulsory voting.

Supporters argue that compulsory voting gives governments a mandate from almost everyone, not just the keenest voters, so politicians have to appeal to the whole country. They say it makes it harder to win by stirring up only your base, and that a small duty every few years is reasonable, pointing to Australia, where it's widely accepted. Want the case against too?
Why do some people prefer first past the post?

Its supporters argue that it's simple to understand, gives every area its own MP who can be voted out, and usually produces one party with enough seats to govern and carry out what it promised. They say proportional systems can give small parties outsized power in coalition deals made after the election. Would you like the case for proportional representation too?

Supporters of proportional representation argue that parliament should reflect how people actually voted, so a party with a fifth of the votes gets about a fifth of the seats. They say it ends safe seats and wasted votes, means people needn't vote tactically, and encourages parties to cooperate, as in Germany or New Zealand. That's the case they make.
What's the case for getting rid of nuclear weapons?

Abolition campaigners argue that nuclear weapons could kill millions in minutes, that near-misses and false alarms show deterrence can fail by accident, and that as long as some countries have them, others will want them. They point to the 2017 treaty banning them, signed by many countries, as the path forward. Would you like the deterrence case as well?
And the case for keeping them?

Supporters of deterrence argue that no two nuclear-armed powers have fought a full war with each other since 1945, and that the threat of unacceptable retaliation is why. They say giving them up while rivals keep theirs would invite pressure or attack, and that disarmament must be mutual and verified. That's the case they make.
Make the case for free university tuition.

Supporters argue that education is a public good, since society gains from more doctors, engineers and teachers, so it should be paid for like schools are. They say debt discourages people from poorer families, and point to countries like Germany and Scotland that manage without fees. Would you like the arguments for charging fees as well?
Give me the case for tariffs, the way their supporters would.

Supporters argue that tariffs protect factories and the towns built around them from being undercut by countries with subsidies or low wages. They say a country needs to make its own steel, chips and medicines in a crisis, and that tariffs are leverage to get fairer trade deals. They accept goods may cost a bit more and say good jobs are worth it. Want the free-trade case too?

Free-trade supporters argue that tariffs are a tax paid by people at home through higher prices, and that other countries hit back with tariffs of their own, hurting exporters. They say open trade lets each country specialise, lifts living standards and has taken millions out of poverty worldwide. That's how they make their case.
Why do some people oppose Medicare for All?

Opponents argue that it would need very large tax increases, that around half of Americans get insurance through work and many like their plans, and that a single government payer could mean longer waits and less innovation. They prefer building on the current mix, such as expanding subsidies. Would you like the supporters' case too?
What were the arguments against raising France's pension age?

Opponents argued that working two more years falls hardest on people in manual jobs, who often start younger and live shorter lives, and that pensions are a hard-won right. They proposed raising money through taxes on high earners or companies instead, and said the change was pushed through parliament without a final vote. Would you like the government's case too?
Yes, why did the government want it?

The government argued that French people live longer and there are fewer workers per retiree, so the pension system would run deficits without changes. It said raising the age was fairer than cutting pensions or raising contributions, and that most neighbouring countries already retire later. That was its case.
Make the case for inheritance tax.

Supporters argue that inheritance is the clearest example of unearned wealth, so taxing it is fairer than taxing work. They say it limits the build-up of dynastic fortunes, that most estates fall below the threshold, and that the money funds services everyone uses. Want the case against as well?

Opponents argue that people already paid tax on that money when they earned it, so taxing it again at death is unfair. They say the wish to leave something for your children is natural, that family farms and businesses can be broken up to pay the bill, and that the wealthiest avoid it with trusts and planning anyway. That's the case they make.
What's the best argument for protecting the green belt?

Its defenders argue that the green belt has stopped cities sprawling into one another for decades, keeping countryside within reach for millions. They say once fields are built on they're gone for good, that farmland and wildlife matter more than ever, and that building on brownfield land and empty homes first is the smarter route. Shall I give you the case for building on some of it?
Argue for strict AI regulation, as its supporters would.

Supporters argue that AI is spreading into hiring, lending, news and weapons faster than society can adapt, and mistakes at that scale are hard to reverse. They want testing before release, clear responsibility when harm happens, labels on AI content and limits on the riskiest uses, much like rules for medicines or aircraft. Would you like the case for a lighter touch?

Supporters of lighter rules argue that AI is improving fast and heavy rules now would freeze today's guesses into law. They say compliance costs favour the biggest companies and push research to countries with fewer rules, and that laws on fraud, discrimination and safety already apply. They prefer targeted rules for proven harms. That's how they put it.
What do people who oppose decriminalising drugs argue?

Opponents argue that removing penalties sends a message that drug use is acceptable, and that without the threat of prosecution fewer people are pushed into treatment. They point to Oregon, which decriminalised in 2020 and brought back penalties in 2024 after public drug use rose. They prefer pairing law enforcement with treatment. Want the supporters' case too?
Make the case for faith schools.

Supporters argue that faith schools give parents a choice that reflects their family's values, often achieve strong results and good behaviour, and have served communities for generations, sometimes long before the state ran schools. They say a shared ethos helps children feel they belong. Would you like the case its critics make as well?
What's the argument for minimum service levels during strikes?

Supporters argue that when ambulance, rail or fire staff strike, the public can be put at risk and people can't get to work, so a basic level of service should continue. They say many European countries already have such rules and that unions can still strike. Would you like the unions' case against them?

Unions argue that minimum service rules quietly take away the right to strike, because if most staff must work anyway, a strike loses its force. They say workers in essential jobs already agree emergency cover voluntarily, and that the real answer to strikes is fair pay and decent staffing. That's how they put it.
Why do some countries think conscription is a good idea?

Countries that use it argue that a large trained reserve deters attack and means the whole society can defend itself, not just a small professional army. Finland is often given as the example. They also argue that serving together mixes people from different backgrounds and builds a shared sense of duty. Would you like the arguments against it too?
Make the case against a generational smoking ban.

Opponents argue that adults should decide for themselves about legal risks, and that a law letting a 40-year-old buy cigarettes but not a 39-year-old is unfair and hard to enforce. They warn that bans feed black markets and that shopkeepers bear the burden. They prefer education, taxes and quitting support. Would you like the supporters' case too?
Why do people want to ban lab-grown meat?

Supporters of bans argue that farming is central to their culture and rural life, and that ultra-processed meat grown in steel tanks isn't proven safe over the long term. They want to protect farmers from competition backed by big investors, and say people should know clearly what they're eating. Would you like the case for lab-grown meat as well?
Why do people want to keep the Autobahn without a speed limit?

Opponents of a general limit argue that the Autobahn is among the safer road networks in Europe per kilometre driven, that limits already apply on risky stretches, and that most drivers choose sensible speeds anyway. They see the open stretches as a matter of personal freedom and a point of national pride. Want the case for a limit too?
What's the case for keeping the US bases in Okinawa?

Supporters argue that the bases are central to the alliance with the United States, which they see as Japan's main guarantee of security, and that Okinawa's location near Taiwan and the East China Sea makes it hard to move them far. They also point to jobs and money the bases bring. Would you like the case Okinawans who want fewer bases make?

Okinawans who want fewer bases argue that their prefecture, a small part of Japan's land, hosts most US military facilities in the country. They point to aircraft noise, accidents and crimes by service members, and to land taken after the war. They want the burden shared across Japan, and many oppose building the new base at Henoko. That's their case.
Why do some people want more police funding?

Supporters argue that police officers prevent and solve crimes, and that cuts mean slower responses and more unsolved cases. They say residents of high-crime neighbourhoods often ask for more patrols, not fewer, and that well-funded forces can afford better training. Would you like the case for moving some money to other services?

People who want to shift funding argue that officers spend much of their time on mental health crises, addiction and homelessness, which trained counsellors and social workers could handle better. They say this would free police for serious crime, prevent harmful encounters and build trust. That's how they put it.
What were the arguments for affirmative action?

Supporters argued that generations of discrimination left some groups with fewer chances, so considering race helped level the field. They said diverse classrooms help everyone learn, and that professions like medicine and law should reflect the people they serve. Would you like the opposing case too?

Opponents argued that treating applicants differently by race is itself discrimination, whatever the aim, and that admissions should judge each person's own merits. They said it disadvantaged some applicants, especially many Asian Americans, and that help should target poverty rather than race. That's the case they made.
Make the case for banning social media for under 16s.

Supporters argue that apps are designed to keep people scrolling, and that young teenagers are especially vulnerable to comparison, bullying and harmful content at a key time for mental health. They say parents can't hold the line alone when every friend is online, so a clear legal age helps everyone, as Australia has tried. Would you like the arguments against too?
Why are some people against term limits?

Opponents argue that term limits take away voters' right to keep someone they think is doing a good job, and push out experienced politicians just as they master the work. They say the people who stay, such as long-serving staff and lobbyists, gain power instead. Would you like the case for term limits too?
What's the case against lowering the voting age?

Opponents argue that eighteen is when most adult rights begin, such as serving on a jury, and voting should match. They say sixteen-year-olds are still at school and mostly not yet paying much tax or living independently, and that a single clear age avoids confusion. Want the case in favour too?
Why do some people want to cut the consumption tax?

Supporters of a cut argue that the tax takes a bigger share of income from lower-income households, since they spend most of what they earn, and that prices have risen sharply. They say a cut, especially on food, would ease the cost of living and boost spending. Would you like the case for keeping or raising it?
Give me the farmers' case against rewilding.

Many farmers argue that good land should grow food, especially when countries import a lot of what they eat. They say bringing back predators puts livestock at risk, that rewilding projects are often decided by distant landowners or charities, and that their families have cared for the land for generations. Would you like the rewilding supporters' case too?
